findings.explanation: high confidence.  Witness: A graph with triangle T = {a, b, c} and start vertex s, where s is adjacent to a and also adjacent to another vertex u not in T, with u adjacent to b. In a BFS from s, if u is processed before a, b is discovered from u (so parent(b) = u != a). Then scanning edge bc does not identify the triangle {a, b, c} in O(1) time (and parent(b) != parent(c)). More generally, two vertices on level 2 connected by an edge need not share a common parent at level 1 (e.g. C_5), so an edge at level 2 does not trivially reveal a triangle in O(1) time without verifying common neighbors, which itself is triangle detection or requires parent tracking that fails when parents differ from a). Consequently, the claim that {a, b, c} is detected when scanning the adjacency list of b does not hold in general in O(1) time per edge without already knowing their common neighbors, which is the very problem being solved. As a result, the O(m^{2/3}n) algorithm and Theorem 2 are invalid; indeed, if true, this would have broken the longstanding combinatorial matrix multiplication barrier via [39]. Thus, Case 2.1 is flawed and the algorithm does not correctly guarantee detection of triangle T in this case. The author assumes without justification that a must be the parent of both b and c in the BFS tree, which fails whenever b or c has other neighbors among the level-1 vertices.

Case 2.1: Exactly one vertex, namely a, appears on level 1. Then b and c appear on the next
level (level 2) of the BFS tree. Assuming that b is discovered before c, the triangle {a, b, c} is
detected while scanning the adjacency list of b. Refer to Fig. 1 (iii).
